title: Three-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model
abstract: The three-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model is investigated using the strong-coupling diagram technique. For half-filling, the boundary between paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic states is determined for the range of the Hubbard repulsion $4t\leq U\leq12t$, where $t$ is the hopping integral between neighboring sites. Along this boundary, the density of states is calculated, and it demonstrates the Mott transition at $U\approx9t$. For $U\geq6t$ and half-filling, the density of states has the shape inherent in the strong electron repulsion, while for $U=4t$, its shape points to weak coupling. The dependence of the Néel temperature $T_{\rm N}$ on the electron concentration $\bar{n}$ is investigated for the cases $U=4t$ and $12t$. In the former case, $T_{\rm N}$ decreases monotonously with $\bar{n}$, while in the latter case, there is a plateau in the dependence near $\bar{n}=0.87$. The plateau is connected to a reconstruction of the density of states caused by an effective weakening of electron coupling due to electron depopulation. For $U=12t$ and half-filling, the magnetic critical exponent $γ\approx1.4$, which is close to the value in the Heisenberg model. Some features resembling the first-order phase transition, revealing themselves in a finite crystal, are discussed.
summary: This work applies the strong-coupling diagram technique to analyze the phase diagram of the 3D repulsive Hubbard model. It determines critical boundaries between paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases while investigating how the density of states evolves across different interaction strengths ($U$). The results highlight complex doping effects, such as plateaus in $T_N$ linked to spectral reconstruction.
main_problem: The study investigates the phase diagram of the three-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model, focusing on the transition between paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic states.
main_result: The analysis reveals a Mott transition in the density of states around $U\approx9t$ and shows that doping dependence of the Néel temperature exhibits plateaus linked to changes in electron coupling strength.
method: The strong-coupling diagram technique (SCDT) is employed, involving series expansion in kinetic energy and solving coupled equations for spin and charge susceptibilities.
model_or_system: The system is the 3D repulsive Hubbard model on a simple cubic lattice, described by the Hamiltonian $	ext{H} = \sum_{\langle l l' angle\sigma} t_{ll'} (a^\dagger_{l'\sigma} a_{l\sigma} + h.c.) + U \sum_l n_{l\uparrow} n_{l\downarrow}$.
key_observables: Néel temperature ($T_N$), Density of States (DOS), magnetic critical exponent ($\gamma$), and spin/charge susceptibilities.
important_parameters: $U$ (Hubbard repulsion) relative to $t$ (hopping integral); electron concentration $ ar{n}$; regimes like $4t \le U \le 12t$.
main_assumptions: The primary method relies on the strong-coupling diagram technique, which is most accurate for the limit where $U \gg t$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the variation of $T_N$ with doping ($ ar{n}$) showing plateaus (e.g., Fig. 6), and demonstrate how the DOS changes from weak-coupling quasiparticle features to strong-coupling Mott gaps depending on $ ar{n}$ and $U$.
paper_structure:
The paper systematically analyzes phase boundaries ($T_N(U)$) using SCDT, calculates susceptibilities via determinant analysis ($\Delta(k, 
u)$), and examines how the DOS and critical exponents change as a function of both interaction strength ($U$) and doping ($ ar{n}$).
why_interesting: The study provides detailed theoretical insights into fundamental many-body physics in strongly correlated electron systems, particularly concerning Mott transitions and magnetic ordering in 3D lattices.

In the former case, the DOS is well separated into an intensive quasiparticle maximum with a dip near ω = 0 originating in part from the Hubbard repulsion and the Slater mechanism [30] and a less intensive higher-frequency electron-spin- excitation continuum. Such a type of DOS is inherent in weak coupling. For U ≥6t, it is difficult to separate the spectrum into these two parts – the case is typical for strong correlations.
